Sequential AIPE Check for the Gini Index

Source: R/seq_aipe_gini.R
seq_aipe_gini.Rd

Checks, with the data collected so far, whether enough observations are in hand for a confidence interval for the population Gini index of inequality (of incomes, wealth, sales, and the like) that is no wider than a chosen width, without assuming a distribution and without a planning value. This is the sequential fixed width interval procedure of Chattopadhyay and De (2016), expressed in the package's accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) form with the full width of the interval as the target.

Usage

seq_aipe_gini(x, width, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector of nonnegative values: the observations collected so far, at least 4 of them. Missing, infinite, or negative values are an error.

width

The target full width of the confidence interval for the Gini index: the upper limit minus the lower limit (twice the half width \(d\) of Chattopadhyay and De, 2016). A single positive number less than 1: the Gini index lies between 0 and 1, so an interval 1 or more wide would say nothing, and such a target is an error.

conf_level

The confidence level of the interval, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with one row per quantity and columns term and value. The rows are, in order:

lower_limit

the lower confidence limit (NA when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed; see the section below);

gini

the estimated Gini index (NA when every value is zero);

upper_limit

the upper confidence limit (NA whenever lower_limit is);

xi_squared

the estimated asymptotic variance \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\), at least \(n^{-3}\) (the bound itself when the estimate is not yet usable);

criterion_n

the sample size the stopping rule currently requires (at least current_n + 1 when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed);

current_n

the current sample size.

The object also carries these attributes:

is_satisfied

TRUE when the stopping rule is met, otherwise FALSE; never NA, and always identical to current_n >= criterion_n;

method

the string "Gini index";

current_n, criterion_n

the values in the rows of those names;

conf_level, width

the values supplied;

variance_unusable

TRUE when the raw variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (see the section below), otherwise FALSE;

notes

a character vector, empty unless something needs explaining.

Details

The function evaluates the stopping rule once and returns. The user collects the pilot sample (see seq_aipe_gini_pilot), calls seq_aipe_gini(), and, while the rule is not met, adds one or more observations and calls it again. The function prints nothing and keeps no state.

Estimate. The Gini index \(G = \Delta / (2\mu)\), with \(\Delta = E|X_1 - X_2|\) Gini's mean difference, is estimated by \(G_n = \hat{\Delta}_n / (2 \bar{X}_n)\), as returned by gini_index. It is defined for nonnegative data with a positive mean, so a negative value in x is an error. A sample in which every value is zero cannot estimate the index; because that can happen by chance in a small early sample, it is reported as "not yet estimable" rather than as an error (see the section below).

Stopping rule. Sampling stops at the first \(n\), at or after the pilot size, with $$n \ge \left\lceil \frac{4 z_{\alpha/2}^2}{\omega^2} \left(\hat{\xi}_n^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \right\rceil,$$ which is the stopping rule of Chattopadhyay and De (2016, Equation 12), \(n \ge (z_{\alpha/2}/d)^2 (V_n^2 + 1/n)\), with \(\omega = 2d\). Here \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) is their estimator \(V_n^2\) (Equation 11) of the asymptotic variance of \(\sqrt{n}(G_n - G)\) (Equation 6), built from the sample mean and variance, the Gini mean difference, a second U-statistic, and a jackknife variance. The reported interval is \(G_n \pm z_{\alpha/2} \hat{\xi}_n / \sqrt{n}\). Whenever the rule is met, the width of that interval is at most width. The article bounds \(V_n^2\) below by zero; the package bounds a positive estimate below by \(n^{-3}\), as for the other effect sizes, and treats an estimate that is zero or negative as not yet usable (see the section below).

Which interval. The interval reported is built as for every effect size in the family, from the estimated standard error. It is not the interval of Chattopadhyay and De (2016), which is the fixed width interval \((G_n - d, G_n + d)\), always exactly \(\omega\) wide, whose coverage their stopping rule is designed to secure. The interval reported is never wider than that one once the rule is met, and it covers less often: in simulated studies with lognormal data, a Gini index of 0.3, and a 95% level (10,000 studies each, the default m_0, one observation added at each stage), the interval reported covered the Gini index in 0.890 of the studies at width = 0.2 and 0.916 at width = 0.1, and the article's interval in 0.986 and 0.960. For the article's interval, take the estimate (the row gini) plus and minus half of width.

Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) cite this procedure and give the general sequential AIPE framework that the rest of the seq_aipe_* family implements; their article does not itself contain a Gini index procedure.

What the guarantee is. The width guarantee is exact. The coverage guarantee is asymptotic: coverage approaches conf_level as width shrinks. In simulated studies with a 95% interval and one observation added at each stage, coverage for exponential data (a Gini index of 0.5) was 0.951 at width = 0.1 (3,000 studies, about 142 observations at the end), 0.937 at width = 0.2 (2,000 studies, about 44 observations), and 0.945 at width = 0.4 (6,000 studies, about 17 observations). For lognormal data with a Gini index of 0.3 it was 0.890 at width = 0.2 (10,000 studies, about 30 observations) and 0.870 at width = 0.4 (about 13 observations). The variance estimate was never zero, negative, or below its lower bound in these studies; the shortfall comes from the small final samples that wide targets allow. Use seq_aipe_gini_sensitivity to study a planned study before collecting data.

Estimates That Are Not Yet Usable

When the raw variance estimate is zero (exactly, or to within rounding error), negative, or not finite, which is common at small sample sizes for some effect sizes, or when the point estimate cannot be computed (a sample with no variation, where values that agree to ten significant digits count as equal), the check reports the stopping rule as not met, sets attr(out, "variance_unusable") to TRUE, and attaches a note that print() shows; see smsd_check_methods. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed in the source articles, under which the lower bound \(n^{-3}\) would stand in for such an estimate and the rule would be met at once with an interval far narrower than requested; a positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe (the larger of it and \(n^{-3}\)).

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & De, S. K. (2016). Estimation of Gini index within pre-specified error bound. Econometrics, 4(3), 30. doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

See also

seq_aipe_gini_pilot for the pilot size, seq_aipe_gini_sensitivity to simulate the procedure before collecting data, and gini_index and gini_mean_diff for the point estimates. (DMAR has no fixed sample size analog for the Gini index.)

Other seq_aipe_gini: seq_aipe_gini_pilot(), seq_aipe_sensitivity

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# How unequal are household incomes (in thousands of dollars) in a
# region? The aim is a 95% confidence interval for the Gini index that
# is no wider than 0.15.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_aipe_gini_pilot(width = 0.15)
income <- rlnorm(m, meanlog = 4, sdlog = 0.6)
out <- seq_aipe_gini(income, width = 0.15)
out
#> Sequential check (Gini index)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 27
#>   Criterion n     : 47
#>   Target width    : 0.15
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.2540293
#>   gini              : 0.3200881
#>   upper_limit       : 0.386147
#>   xi_squared        : 0.03067111
#>   criterion_n       : 47
#>   current_n         : 27
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one household at a time and check
# again, until it is.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  income <- c(income, rlnorm(1, meanlog = 4, sdlog = 0.6))
  out <- seq_aipe_gini(income, width = 0.15)
}
out
#> Sequential check (Gini index)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 47
#>   Criterion n     : 47
#>   Target width    : 0.15
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.2835468
#>   gini              : 0.3452086
#>   upper_limit       : 0.4068704
#>   xi_squared        : 0.04651941
#>   criterion_n       : 47
#>   current_n         : 47
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
